name: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
statement: Each additional unit of something gives you less extra satisfaction than the one before.
statementAccent: less extra satisfaction than the one before
meaning: As you consume more of a good within a given period, holding all else constant, the extra satisfaction from each further unit declines. The first slice of pizza when hungry is intensely satisfying; the fourth much less so. It concerns the marginal satisfaction of the next unit, not the total, which usually keeps rising, just more slowly.
mechanism: Wants for any single good are satiable. As consumption rises, the most urgent uses are satisfied first, and successive units go to progressively lower-valued uses, so each adds less. The claim presupposes that tastes, income, and prices are held fixed and that there is no time gap to renew appetite. It is a behavioural and introspective generalisation about preferences, not a result derived from any deeper physical law.

examples.text: The first glass of water to a thirsty person, or the first slice of pizza, delivers high satisfaction; each further one delivers less, until satiety brings the marginal value to zero or below.
Water is essential yet cheap, diamonds useless yet dear — resolved by noting that value tracks marginal, not total, utility: abundant water has low marginal utility, scarce diamonds high.
The same sum means more to a poor person than a rich one, a common motivation for progressive taxation — though this use rests on comparing utility across people, itself a contested step.

variants.name: Gossen's second law
variants.text: The equimarginal principle: a consumer maximises satisfaction by allocating spending so that the marginal utility per unit of money is equal across all goods.

variants.name: The diminishing marginal rate of substitution
variants.text: The modern ordinal-utility reframing, which replaces cardinal 'diminishing marginal utility' with a statement about how consumers trade one good off against another.

whyItMatters: It is the foundation on which the marginal revolution rebuilt the theory of value, explaining downward-sloping demand and resolving the ancient paradox of value. It remains a central teaching idea in microeconomics, even as its formal underpinnings have shifted from cardinal toward ordinal utility.

working.lead: Value the next unit, not the total
working.text: when weighing more of a good, judge the extra satisfaction of the next unit, which falls as you already have more.
use marginal utility to see why abundant essentials can be cheap and scarce trinkets dear.
remember the law assumes fixed tastes and no renewed appetite, and that comparing utility across people is a further, contested step.

limits: It is a foundational generalisation with documented exceptions, not a universal law — some goods show increasing marginal utility over a range, such as a course of antibiotics whose sub-therapeutic doses help less than proportionally, or a collector completing a set. Its very formulation depends on the contested notion of cardinally measurable utility; modern ordinal-utility theory holds that utility can only be ranked, not measured, and reframes the idea as a diminishing marginal rate of substitution. Its claimed grounding in the psychophysical Weber-Fechner law is disputed. Utility itself is subjective and unobservable, so critics see the law as closer to a tractable assumption than an established empirical fact.
misreadings: It does not say total satisfaction falls as you consume more — usually the total keeps rising; it is the extra satisfaction per unit that declines. And it is not an exceptionless law: some goods, over some ranges, deliver increasing marginal utility.
origin: First stated systematically by the German economist Hermann Heinrich Gossen in 1854, as what is now called Gossen's first law; ignored in his lifetime and rediscovered when Jevons, Menger, and Walras independently made diminishing marginal utility the basis of value theory in the 1870s.
